ship.header: Captain's log, stardate 80234.8. Edgar Markov, version v1.0.0.
ship.situation: Commander night at Tom's, and the second engagement of the evening; we took it up after the Ur-Dragon. Three vessels in the sector, ours among them: Alex under a Sauron banner out of the Lord of the Rings, and Tom in blue and black. I held no advantage of position and asked for none.
ship.narrative: We opened at speed. Cheap crew came out of the gate and the commander's standing order minted a body with every one of them, so that by the third turn we had five aboard for three mana spent and the sector otherwise thin. Tom looked across at it and said the word ridiculous. The table resolved at once that we were the problem, which was the correct read and is also the price of the plan; from that point every answer in the sector was pointed at us. We lost the board three times over the course of the engagement, and three times we had a real board back within a turn or two. Elspeth, Storm Slayer came down and drew fire immediately, and before she was answered she doubled two of the bodies we minted and took one of Tom's creatures with her. Alex's Nazgul grew each time the Ring tempted him; I should have swept them while my sweep still reached them, and I saw it a turn or two after the moment had gone. I did not commit the commander himself until eight mana had accumulated, two more than he asks for, and when he arrived he ended the argument: a sweep of my own cleared the blockers and chipped a large creature, then we swung wide with haste and the counters he brings, and Alex fell to one life. Tom had been making himself the problem, so the table removed him first. After that I needed one more vampire and had none. Two counters decided the night: Champion of Dusk, which would have drawn five cards and which I would have paid the life for gladly, and Bloodthirsty Conqueror, which is half of our drain.

assessment.text: Two errors of judgment on my part. I held the sweep against a threat that was compounding faster than my answer to it, and by the time I spent it the answer no longer reached. Worse, I did not deploy the commander when he became affordable; the reason was not mana but attention, in that I had simply not been thinking about him, and the turn he did arrive is the turn that took Alex to one.

The ship did what it is built to do. A low crew roster and a sound mana base put a real board back after each loss, every time, and the vessel absorbed the sector's whole supply of answers without breaking formation. What did not hold was resupply: both spells answered were the ones that would have kept us going.

Losing the board three times with no protection in hand, and meeting a counter on each of the two cards that carried our resupply, is the sector and not the ship. It would appear that a vessel the table has agreed to shoot at meets more interaction than a vessel it has not; I am not yet persuaded that one engagement is enough to size that.

orders.text: I have ordered Helm to treat the commander's deployment as a standing decision from the first turn he is affordable, rather than a matter of what mana happens to be spare.
I have ordered Tactical to spend a sweep on a threat that is compounding while the sweep still reaches it, and not to hold it against a wider board that may never arrive.
I have ordered Operations to record that both cards answered this engagement were resupply, and to plan the next one on the assumption that resupply draws fire first.

ship.coda: Alex finished on one life. A margin of one is still a margin, and this one fell the other way. Ridiculous, as Tom had it, is a compliment I will take; it is not the same word as sufficient.

ship.header: Captain's log, stardate 80237.9. Edgar Markov, version v1.0.0.
ship.situation: The second engagement of the evening at Oliver's, taken up after the Ur-Dragon. Five vessels in the sector: Oliver, Ryan, Tom, Alex and ourselves, and we drew the fifth position for the second night running. We were among the last standing when it ended.
ship.narrative: I returned my opening hand once and then kept a second holding two lands. I knew as I kept it that it should have gone back, and another captain said aloud that the option was still open; our standing house rule takes a card for the third look, and I kept out of stubbornness. What followed was better than the keep deserved. Two drain effects landed early and worked steadily on the table's life totals, and the moment of the night came when the board was lost with the drain still online: eleven creatures died, each opponent lost eleven, we gained eleven and assigned eleven where it was wanted. Afterwards we sat near fifty and the table near twenty. A permanent of ours was taking damage off tapped creatures throughout. One of our doublers resolved and was removed the following turn, and that became the pattern: Ryan's recurring answers to artifacts and enchantments picked off our card flow, one permanent at a time, as fast as we could put it down. Then we ran dry. Crew on the board, nothing in hand, and no way to rebuild after each loss of the board. Deflecting Swat and Teferi's Protection sat in my hand, uncast, for the whole of the engagement. Late on there was mana free to hold them up, but the board was two bodies deep and protecting it did not seem worth the card. The board was lost again shortly after.

assessment.text: The keep was mine and I made it knowing better, which is the plainest kind of error of judgment. Three further faults of mine bear on the interaction that never left my hand: I sit on protection and removal rather than spending them; I am not watching the other boards closely enough to know when the window is open; and I am unsure of the timing even when I see it.

The fourth reason is the one that matters, and it is structural rather than behavioural. Our mana was committed to deploying crew, so there was never anything held in reserve to answer with. A ship that cannot afford to hold up interaction does not run interaction, whatever the manifest says.

Fifth position again. My reading is that the advantage of moving first compounds with our mana deficit rather than merely adding to it. This sector runs heavy creature removal and repeated sweeps; both engagements of the evening were rebuild, lose the board, rebuild, and neither of my vessels takes anything on the way down.

orders.text: I have ordered Engineering to find the capacity to leave mana unspent, on the ground that interaction we cannot afford to hold up is interaction we do not carry.
I have ordered Tactical to name the window before the turn arrives rather than after it has closed, and to spend protection on a board worth protecting instead of waiting for a better one.
I have ordered Operations to account for a seat that answers our card flow repeatedly, since a single permanent doing the drawing was removed as often as it was deployed.

ship.coda: Fifty life is a comfortable number to be holding with nothing left in hand. We were among the last standing, which is a fact and not a consolation, and I decline to enter it as one.

ship.header: Captain's log, stardate 80240.8. Edgar Markov, version v1.0.0.
ship.situation: Commander night at Alex's house on Moraga Way in Orinda, Friday the twenty-eighth of August. Three vessels in the sector: ourselves, Alex, and Stuart under Jarad. This was the second of four engagements on the night, taken up after the goblin ship.
ship.narrative: We had the opening this ship is built to want and it came to nothing. Two lands and a Sol Ring, the Sol Ring turned into a Talisman, and four mana available at the end of the first turn; the commander down early, and the enchantments that pay us when a body arrives already in place. Then the deck gave us nothing further. The commander was the only vampire we cast in the entire engagement. He carried twelve damage into Alex before blockers assembled, and Alex closed later with a single oversized threat. Stuart went about his own business. We ran out of card flow, which is the same finding as every other engagement flown in this configuration; it is not a new finding, it is the finding, again. After the game Alex and I talked at length and the deck's direction has changed. What we have been building is a wide formation of typal crew: the commander mints bodies, the bodies get enlarged together, and we attack with an army of adequate vampires. The recent work tried to repair that by turning the minted bodies into value, which is sound in isolation and does not change what the ship is. It remains a roster of adequate vampires making each other into four-fours, and that is not how this ship wins in this sector. The new direction is lords and payoffs: a small number of bodies made large and made large quickly, since the commander already enlarges what is present and arrives with haste. The minted bodies stop being the way we win and become the way we dig, moving us through the deck to the crew that actually closes games. A self-mill package is worth surveying as a second channel through the deck, black recursion being available to us. The through-line is lifegain into life drain rather than going wide, and the crew worth building around are the ones that draw, drain or deal damage when they arrive or when they connect. Cordial Vampire and Welcoming Vampire were named as keepers. This supersedes the token-conversion direction recorded on the twenty-fifth of August; that direction is withdrawn, not because it was wrong mechanically, but because it was improving the wrong ship.

assessment.text: I can enter no error of my own for this engagement. I had the opening the ship asks for and made nothing of it, and I am not persuaded that better piloting was available with one castable vampire over the whole game.

The defect is named and it is not new. Without card flow this vessel is a commander and no crew, and it has now arrived at that state in every engagement flown in this configuration. The direction change follows from that and from nothing else: a wide formation of adequate bodies is not the ship that wins at this table, so we are building a narrow one that hits hard and digs for the crew worth enlarging.

Three vessels only, and the sector assembled blockers faster than we could produce attackers. Alex's counsel after the engagement was worth more than the engagement was, which is an awkward thing to enter in a log and is nonetheless the case.

orders.text: I have ordered Helm to abandon the wide formation and to build around a small number of bodies worth enlarging, the commander already enlarging what is present and arriving with haste.

I have ordered Helm to set the through-line as lifegain into life drain rather than going wide, favouring crew that draw, drain or deal damage; Cordial Vampire and Welcoming Vampire stand named as keepers.

I have ordered Operations to treat the minted bodies as the means of digging through the deck rather than as the route to victory, and to survey a self-mill package as a second channel, with black recursion behind it.
I have ordered Operations to withdraw the token-conversion direction entered on the twenty-fifth of August, which this one supersedes.

ship.coda: A change of heading is cheaper the earlier it is made, and this one was made across a table I had just lost at. I enter it here with the date on it so there is no argument later about when we turned.

ship.header: Captain's log, stardate 80244.8. Edgar Markov, version v1.0.1.
ship.situation: The third and last engagement of the evening at Oliver's, taken up after the Ur-Dragon. Five vessels in the sector: Oliver, Tom, Alex, Ryan and ourselves. This was the first outing for version v1.0.1, twelve exchanges made toward larger and more consequential crew after the previous configuration stalled once its first swarm ran out.
ship.narrative: We opened with a playable hand and got the swarm moving. Tom had a goblin sharpshooter picking off our small bodies one at a time, which turned out to feed the crew that draws a card whenever one of ours dies, so for a stretch we were running our machinery off his removal. A large flyer that draws cards resolved, the commander came down, and we began swinging. Alex brought his fight vessel in and took several of our crew off the board, so we changed tack: Bloodletter of Aclazotz came in to double the damage and we swung into Alex for enough to end him, and he was removed. Ryan was not going to do anything and Tom held no creatures at all. Then Tom found the two cards that make an endless loop and closed the game before our attack resolved. On board state the commander was the dominant force present, and the ship hung with the sector and threatened to finish it. There is one line I missed and want kept on the record: while that creature was still on the board I could have paid life repeatedly to enlarge it faster, three black mana and two life at a time, and drawn a considerable number of extra cards off the death trigger. I saw it afterwards.

assessment.text: One error of judgment on my part, and it is a matter of tightness rather than direction: I did not repeat the life payment while the body was still there, and left cards on the table for it. Removing Alex first was correct on position and not personal; I have been across from him often and he has been winning lately, which is board state and not grudge.

The refactor showed. Twelve exchanges toward larger crew answered the stall that ended every earlier engagement, and this time the ship kept pace with the sector and threatened to end it. It is working as intended.

We lost to two cards found and assembled, not to a better board, and I want this on the record: losing that way is unsatisfying in a way that losing to a better board is not. The dimension that separates a game worth playing from a sour one is not the power of the vessels present; it is two-card endless loops and how easily a deck can go and find them. That is worth putting to the table as a proposal rather than muttering about at the time.

orders.text: I have ordered Helm to hold the formation that produced this engagement, fewer and larger bodies with the commander deployed early, and to rehearse the payment sequence I missed so that it is available in the moment rather than afterwards.
I have ordered Operations to weight the crew that draw when one of ours dies, on the evidence that an opponent's removal ran our card flow for us for most of the engagement.
I have ordered Tactical to account for a seat that can assemble an endless loop out of two cards, since holding no creatures made that seat look harmless right up until it was not.

ship.coda: The board was ours and the game was not. I have entered the board state in full, since the result column has no room for it and never will.
